name: RBC indices
seoDesc: RBC indices: work out mean corpuscular volume (MCV) from the hemoglobin and the hematocrit. A free health calculator with the formula, units and a worked…
summary: mean corpuscular volume (MCV) is what the RBC indices calculator works out, and it gets there from the hemoglobin, the hematocrit and the RBC count. It suits an informed starting point to take to a clinician, not a diagnosis. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the RBC indices calculator work?
sections.html:
The RBC indices calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports mean corpuscular volume (MCV) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case; then you type in the hemoglobin (Hgb), the hematocrit (Hct) and the RBC count.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• Pick the option that matches your case — 2 options, such as female and male. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A number, expressed in g/dL.
  • A number, expressed in %.
  • A number, expressed in million cells/mcL.

1 field on this form is a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: What are the variables at a glance?
sections.html:
Everything the page asks for and everything it reports, side by side. The roles matter: a value you supply is read from the form, a calculated value is derived from the others and cannot be set directly.

FieldWhat it isUnitRole
Hemoglobin (Hgb)A number stated in g/dL.—You supply it
Hematocrit (Hct)A number stated in %.—You supply it
RBC countA number stated in million cells/mcL.—You supply it
Mean corpuscular hemoglobin (MCH)A number stated in pg/cell.—Calculated
Mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (MCHC)A number stated in g/dL.—Calculated
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)A number stated in fl.—Calculated

sections.title: The formula behind the RBC indices calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)=(10 × hematocrit (Hct) ÷ RBC count)
Mean corpuscular hemoglobin (MCH)=(10 × hemoglobin (Hgb) ÷ RBC count)
Mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (MCHC)=(100 × hemoglobin (Hgb) ÷ hematocrit (Hct))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose I am a set to female, Hemoglobin (Hgb) = 10, Hematocrit (Hct) = 10 and RBC count = 10. Working through the relationship above gives Mean corpuscular hemoglobin (MCH) = 10, Mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (MCHC) = 100 and Mean corpuscular volume (MCV) = 10.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Mean corpuscular hemoglobin (MCH) = 10, Mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (MCHC) = 100 and Mean corpuscular volume (MCV) = 10 should be roughly the size you expected from I am a set to female and Hemoglobin (Hgb) = 10.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The RBC indices calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Preparing for an appointment so you can describe your numbers clearly
  • Tracking a measurement over time and understanding what changed
  • Deciding whether a reading is worth a second look
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the hemoglobin, the hematocrit and the RBC count — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.

sections.title: What are the limits worth knowing?
sections.html:
Every tool draws a boundary somewhere. For the RBC indices calculator, these are the ones that matter:

  • The 1 drop-down on this page offers a fixed list of cases. A value that is not on the list cannot be entered, and the nearest option is not always a good substitute.
  • The calculator reports what the relationship implies; it does not judge whether the inputs themselves are sensible, so a figure that is out by a factor of ten will produce an answer that is out by the same factor.

faq.q: What does the RBC indices calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns mean corpuscular volume (MCV), derived from the hemoglobin, the hematocrit and the RBC count. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the RBC indices calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the hemoglobin, the hematocrit and the RBC count, which is 4 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Mean corpuscular hemoglobin (MCH) = 10. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the RBC indices calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
